accuracy.evidence: Standards wording checked against CCSS ELA SL.4.4 (report on a topic or text, tell a story, or recount an experience in an organized manner, using appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details; speak clearly at an understandable pace) and SL.5.4 (sequence ideas logically), and the spoken language aims of the national curriculum in England. Hedgehog facts (eat beetles, worms and slugs; roll into a ball when threatened; hibernate in winter in leaf nests; thousands of spines; live in hedgerows and gardens; forage at night) match the British Hedgehog Preservation Society fact sheet. The 110–160 words-a-minute band is hedged with 'about' and sits around Hasbrouck & Tindal (2017) Grade 4–5 oral reading fluency medians (about 133–146 wcpm) and the ~150 wpm conversational average from the National Center for Voice and Speech. Every pace calculation in the lab and items was checked (130 words at 130 wpm = 60 s; 300 words at 160 wpm = 113 s, so it cannot fit 1 minute).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the common faults teachers report in pupils' talks: opinions offered as facts (two opinion cards, prediction 1, challenge q1, m2), drifting off topic (two off-topic cards, the x-type detail options), facts in random order (grouping step), recounts that open with the exciting moment or jump ahead (step 3 feedback distinguishes a missing orientation, an early ending and a later event; prediction 3), vague details such as nice, fun or really good (step 4, challenge q3), and racing to fit an overlong talk (talk 3 forces 'Cut facts', challenge q4, m3).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagrecount is built on planning a spoken report and recount: sorting cards into use or leave out by fact/opinion/topic, filling three sub-topic groups, building a recount by tapping the next event (orientation first), choosing a sensory detail, and a words-a-minute slider whose face, talk time (words ÷ pace) and Cut facts button decide whether a talk is clear and on time. No other lab has a speaking-pace model; the lab_distinct gate passed under 30% against every flagship lab, including the ordering and opinion labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner finds each rule by acting on it: keeping 'cutest' returns 'That is an opinion: not everyone would agree. A report gives facts you can check'; tapping the coach event first returns 'Start with who, where and when'; tapping the ending early returns 'Save it for the end'; choosing 'It was nice' names it as vague; talk 3 shows that even 160 wpm cannot fit 300 words into a minute and offers cutting instead, and the pace readout shows talk time change as the dot moves.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong answers: 'yes, it is about hedgehogs' for the cutest card (the first opinion card is rejected from the report), 'the most exciting part' first in a recount (the first tap must be the who-where-when line), and 'It was really good' as the more helpful detail (rejected as vague on the first detail sentence). A.reveal names the learner's locked-in pick when each task completes.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five challenge questions with ten wrong-answer messages that name the slip: opinion vs fact, off topic, opening with the funniest moment, putting the ending first, vague 'nice', a detail everyone already knows, talking fast to fit 280 words, overrunning the time, 1 minute (240 ÷ 120 confused) and 4 minutes (multiplying instead of dividing).

readability.evidence: learn/readability.py: kid FK grade 2.1 (family limit 5.0), adult 9.6 (limit 10.0). Kid paragraphs use one concrete example each (hedgehogs eat worms vs are cute; looks/eats/lives groups; first, next, after that, finally; the waves crashed over our feet). Standard codes and the fluency research stay in the adult text; canvas prompts are single short lines.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one move (facts not opinions, grouping, recount order, details and pace); the adult text gives the standards, the structure of each text type, named mistakes with the pace hedge, and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler phrases, and the explanation is under 12% similar to every other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android screenshots in light and dark for all six steps and wrong-answer states (keeping an opinion, a fact dropped in the wrong group, the coach event tapped first, a vague detail, a too-fast talk). After moving the recount pile up and showing only the last placed event, five event cards of at least 44 px fit on the canvas at the taller 1.3 ratio; group boxes keep their titles readable at 97 px wide. Walkthrough passed on iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button: 'Use this card in my report' / 'Leave this card out', 'Put the fact in What it eats', 'Next: First, we got on the coach at school.', 'Add: Ducks paddled over...', and Slower / Faster / Try the talk / Cut facts for the pace slider, so no drag is required. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action (including the pace value), challenge feedback is a role=status live region, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
